# A Mamdani fuzzy inference framework for graded pure-tone audiometric classification: development, validation and open-source implementation

## Abstract {.unnumbered}

**Background and Objective.** Pure-tone audiometry is summarised by the pure-tone average and graded against fixed severity boundaries, which forces a binary verdict on thresholds that carry graded information. A Mamdani fuzzy inference system was developed to return a continuous index, and validated against the WHO PTA-4 schema.

**Methods.** Three NHANES cycles administering air-conduction audiometry to adults aged 20 to 69 years were combined and split at the participant level. Six trapezoidal membership functions were constructed as a Ruspini partition, so memberships sum to one at every threshold, and a 47-rule Mamdani system produced a Fuzzy Audiometric Index. Agreement was assessed by weighted kappa, stratification by distance from a boundary, decision-curve analysis, and a probabilistic benchmark scored by Brier score, log loss and calibration error.

**Results.** Among 19,568 ears from 9,832 adults, the FAI achieved kappa 0.946 against the reference grade, 96.5% overall agreement and a mean absolute error of 4.35 dB, with 99.1% agreement for clear cases and 85.1% within 5 dB of a boundary. An ordinal logistic model recovered the reference grade exactly in all 3,912 test ears with a Brier score of zero, establishing that the reference label is a deterministic thresholding of its input. 

**Conclusions.** The framework reproduces the reference classification while preserving the gradation that crisp thresholds discard. Because the reference label is a deterministic function of the pure-tone average, agreement cannot evidence the graded representation's value, and the probabilistic metrics are where the comparison carries information.

**Keywords:** audiometry, hearing loss classification, fuzzy inference, Ruspini partition, reproducibility, clinical decision support

# Introduction

Pure-tone audiometry remains the primary quantitative assessment of hearing, reporting thresholds at octave and inter-octave frequencies from 0.25 to 8 kHz. In clinical and epidemiological practice these seven or eight values are condensed into a single pure-tone average and graded against fixed boundaries, most commonly the WHO PTA-4 classification of 1997: normal, mild, moderate, moderately severe, severe and profound [@who1997]. The convention is useful precisely because it is simple, and it is now embedded in reporting standards, disability assessment and hearing-aid candidacy criteria worldwide.

Its limitations are equally well established. A continuous quantity is forced into six discrete bins, so a difference of one decibel can change a diagnosis while a clinically meaningful difference within a bin is invisible. The boundaries are administrative rather than physiological: the ±5 dB test-retest variability of audiometry exceeds the distance between adjacent categories at some thresholds, so many ears sit within measurement noise of a verdict. The PTA also discards configuration, so a flat loss and a notched one can share an average while implying different pathologies and prognoses, and a label cannot express trajectory.

Approaches that soften these boundaries have been proposed. Machine-learning classifiers predict the severity grade directly but predict the same crisp categories and are not inspectable [@achakulvisut2025]; preclinical work in the same vein detects cochlear synaptopathy in mice from auditory brainstem responses [@ceriani2025], a different task from grading a human audiogram. Data-driven profiling recovers auditory phenotypes without offering an interpretable decision [@saak2022; @saak2025]. These methods answer a different question: the difficulty is not predicting the label more accurately but representing the underlying quantity so it preserves gradation and remains legible to a clinician.

Fuzzy set theory is a natural fit for that requirement. Membership functions express partial belonging rather than binary assignment, and a Mamdani inference system [@mamdani1975] expresses the decision rules in linguistic terms a clinician can read and modify. Fuzzy approaches have been applied across clinical diagnosis since their introduction [@adlassnig1986] and more recently to EEG-based dementia staging [@amezquita2021], but no published system integrates severity classification, configuration typing, asymmetry grading and temporal tracking in one inspectable framework validated on population-level audiometric data.

This study develops such a framework and validates it on a large nationally representative cohort. The objectives were to construct severity membership functions forming a formal Ruspini partition; to validate the index on a held-out test set with a participant-level split; to benchmark its graded output against probabilistic multi-class models using proper scoring rules; to determine empirically how the width of the graded region affects agreement; and to establish how far the results depend on the classification schema rather than on the method.

# Materials and Methods

## Study Design and Data Source

This was a cross-sectional secondary analysis of audiometric data from three National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) cycles that administered air-conduction pure-tone audiometry to adults aged 20-69 years: 1999–2000 (AUX1), 2011–2012 (AUX_G) and 2015–2016 (AUX_I). Thresholds were recorded at 500, 1000, 2000, 3000, 4000, 6000 and 8000 Hz in each ear.

## Study Sample and Data Cleaning

Ears with NHANES sentinel codes (666 no response at maximum output, 777 refused, 888 could not obtain, 999 did not come) and missing-value placeholders were excluded, and the valid range was clipped to −10 to 120 dB HL. Ears with complete thresholds at all seven frequencies formed the analysis set.

## Train–Test Split

The clean-ear dataset was split at the participant level into training (80%) and held-out test (20%) sets, so both ears of a participant remained in the same partition and bilateral correlation could not leak across the split; the split used a fixed seed and no stratification. Membership functions, optimization, rule development and FAI-to-label calibration were performed on the training set alone, and all reported metrics on the held-out test set.

## Membership Function Construction

Thresholds were assigned to six severity categories and a trapezoidal membership function [a, b, c, d] was fitted per category on percentile criteria, with cores at b = P25 and c = P75 across all training-set thresholds. The categories follow the Clark scheme at 25, 40, 55, 70 and 90 dB HL [@clark1981], the convention in most clinical reporting. WHO's own grade tables use five categories at 20 dB steps [@who1991; @who1997] and its 2021 revision uses seven at 15 dB steps [@who2021]; the 2021 schema was validated alongside and is reported as a companion analysis.

The six trapezoids were arranged as a formal Ruspini partition, so their memberships sum to exactly 1 at every point of the 0 to 120 dB universe and no threshold is unclassified. Retaining the percentile cores, each trapezoid's left foot was set to the previous category's core end and its right foot to the next category's core start, making adjacent shoulders complementary linear ramps that cross at 0.5 at the midpoint of the core gap.

A partition's transition width equals its core gap, which a data-driven fit can leave narrower than the ±5 dB test-retest variability the graded region represents. The construction therefore accepts a minimum transition width, set to 10 dB by widening the gaps while preserving the partition property; this floor was evaluated by ablation.

## Configuration and Asymmetry Fuzzification

Audiogram slope, the decibel change from 500 Hz to 4 kHz, was fuzzified into five categories: Rising (< −5 dB), Flat (−5 to 12 dB), Gently Sloping (12–28 dB), Steeply Sloping (28–45 dB) and Precipitous (>45 dB). A notch module quantifies the 4 kHz dip relative to the mean of the 2 kHz and 8 kHz thresholds, fuzzified into No Notch, Shallow Notch (<15 dB) and Deep Notch (≥15 dB).

Inter-aural asymmetry was fuzzified into Symmetric (≤15 dB), Mildly (16–30 dB), Moderately (31–45 dB) and Severely Asymmetric (>45 dB). The operational criterion is the maximum absolute difference across frequencies, which is more sensitive than either definition used by Suen et al., who applied a pure-tone-average difference above 15 dB and a contiguous-frequency criterion [@suen2021]; no standard criterion for asymmetry exists.

## Fuzzy Inference System

A Mamdani-type fuzzy inference system [@mamdani1975] was constructed with 42 expert-derived rules in three functional groups: 12 severity rules mapping fuzzified thresholds to the severity output, 14 configuration rules classifying audiogram shape, and 4 complex-interaction rules for contour presentations the severity group does not capture. A further 12 rules map inter-aural asymmetry to a separate referral output rather than to severity, since asymmetry indicates unilateral pathology rather than a poorer-hearing ear. The 42-rule base serves both single-ear and bilateral input, so the validated configuration and the deployed one coincide; under the single-ear protocol the asymmetry input is zero and the referral output is inert.

Inference used max–min composition, fuzzy union aggregation and centroid defuzzification to obtain a continuous Fuzzy Audiometric Index (FAI) on a 0 to 100 scale. The severity rules take the PTA-4 speech-frequency average as their primary threshold input, matching the reference standard; this keeps the FAI comparable to the standard against which it is validated, but means agreement with PTA-4 is partly by construction. Frequency-resolved information enters through the slope, notch and asymmetry inputs and through the per-frequency membership vectors.

## Probabilistic Comparator Models

Because a crisp label carries no graded information, the fuzzy output was benchmarked against probabilistic multi-class models scored by proper scoring rules rather than agreement alone. The FAI's graded output is its six Ruspini memberships evaluated at the primary threshold. Those values are non-negative and sum to one, so they constitute a probability distribution over severity and can be scored as one.

Two feature sets were used. The primary threshold alone matches the information the fuzzy severity rules consume, while the seven frequency thresholds provide the full audiogram and contain the four thresholds defining the reference label. Six models were fitted on training data and evaluated on the test set: proportional-odds ordinal logistic regression [@mccullagh1980] and multinomial logistic regression on each feature set, plus gradient boosting and a random forest on the seven-frequency set, scored by multi-class Brier score, log loss, expected calibration error and quadratic-weighted kappa. A uniform distribution provided a reference floor.

## Comparator Schemas

The categories are a labelling convention rather than part of the method, so the pipeline was rebuilt under the WHO 2021 schema (seven categories at 20, 35, 50, 65, 80 and 95 dB HL) using the same cohort, split, core fitting, construction and calibration. The two arms differ only in schema. The six-category system was additionally scored against the 2021 reference, quantifying the cost of a mismatch between fitted categories and the boundaries claimed.

## Evaluation Metrics

Primary metrics were weighted Cohen's κ (quadratic weights), mean absolute error, and agreement stratified by borderline (±5 dB of a boundary) versus clear-case (≥6 dB) status. Bland-Altman analysis compared FAI with PTA-4 after a linear transfer fitted on the training partition mapped the index onto the decibel scale. Per-class sensitivity, specificity and precision were reported to expose the contribution of the majority class to the aggregate figures.

Decision-curve analysis [@vickers2006] compared FAI-based with PTA-4-based referral across threshold probabilities from 0.05 to 0.30, with the risk model fitted on the training partition. For each threshold probability t, net benefit was TP/n − FP/n × t/(1−t), with treat-all and treat-none providing reference curves, and two outcomes were evaluated.

## Temporal Tracking

The NHANES cycles analysed here are repeated cross-sectional surveys with no repeat audiometry on any participant, so no longitudinal audiometric sub-cohort could be constructed and the temporal tracking module, which applies fuzzy-adapted ASHA ototoxicity criteria to FAI trajectories, is demonstrated on illustrative scenarios (Figure S2).

## Statistical Analysis and Software

Analyses used Python: scikit-fuzzy v0.5.0 for inference, scikit-learn v1.9 and statsmodels v0.14 for the comparators, SciPy v1.18 for testing. The complete analysis, including the membership construction, pipeline and verification scripts, is provided as executable open-source code.

## Ethics Statement

No ethics approval was required for this secondary analysis of de-identified, publicly available data.

# Results

## Cohort Characteristics

The cohort comprised 10,889 adults aged 20-69 years (mean 43.9). After exclusions, 19,568 ears from 9,832 adults had complete air-conduction thresholds at all seven frequencies: 15,656 ears (7,866 participants) in the training set and 3,912 (1,966 participants) in the test set. Thresholds were right-skewed with a floor effect at 0 to 10 dB HL, and mean thresholds rose from 11.2 dB HL at 500 Hz to 27.4 dB HL at 8 kHz, consistent with age-related and noise-induced high-frequency loss in a working-age sample. Under the WHO PTA-4 classification [@who1997], 88.1% of ears were normal, 8.7% mild, 2.2% moderate, 0.6% moderately severe, 0.3% severe and 0.1% profound, 

Nearly one in five ears (18.7%) fell within ±5 dB of a boundary, where crisp classification is least certain.

## Membership Function Construction

The percentile-based optimization produced the Ruspini-partition functions shown in Figure 1 (parameters in Table S2), with transition bands of 13.6, 10.0, 10.0, 10.0 and 11.2 dB from normal to profound. Verification confirmed the memberships sum to 1 at every sampled threshold across the 0 to 120 dB universe, with a maximum deviation of zero. The FAI-to-label thresholds calibrated at 23.8, 48.9, 63.8, 66.4 and 95.0.

## Classification Agreement with the Reference Grade

On the test set the FAI achieved weighted Cohen's κ = 0.946 against the Clark PTA-4 grade, with 96.5% overall agreement and a mean absolute error of 4.35 dB. Agreement 99.1% for clear cases (≥6 dB from a boundary) and 85.1% within the borderline zone (±5 dB, 18.7% of test ears). Spearman's correlation was 0.812, restricted in range because 86.9% of test ears are normal and the upper tail is compressed; kappa and MAE are therefore the more direct agreement measures.

Per-class performance is given in Table 1. Sensitivity was 0.980 for normal and 0.950 for mild but fell to 0.621 for moderate and 0.500 for moderately severe loss, macro-averaged sensitivity was 0.786 against the 96.5% overall figure, which the normal majority largely determines. Of 138 disagreements, 104 moved upward by one grade and 34 downward, a predominantly upward error structure that increases false-positive referrals.

## Agreement and Distance from the Severity Boundary

Agreement recovered monotonically with distance from the nearest boundary (Figure 2b): 85.1% within ±5 dB, 90.1% at 10 dB and 93.5% at 15 dB. Bland-Altman analysis (Figure 2a) compared the FAI with PTA-4 after a linear transfer fitted on the training partition mapped the index onto the decibel scale, FAI = 0.890 x PTA + 3.11 (r = 0.887): mean difference +0.25 dB with 95% limits of agreement −11.2 to +11.7 dB, with a proportionate bias widening by 0.13 dB per decibel of mean level.

## Probabilistic Comparison with Machine-Learning Models

Table 2 reports the probabilistic benchmark. A proportional-odds ordinal logistic regression on the primary threshold alone reproduced the reference grade exactly in all 3,912 test ears, with a Brier score and log loss of 0.0000, and the same model on all seven frequencies performed identically. The reference label is therefore not a prediction target but a deterministic thresholding of the pure-tone average, so agreement metrics cannot discriminate between models here: any model able to represent monotone thresholds recovers the label exactly, and residual differences measure how well each approximation fits a step function.

Among the models that do not saturate, the FAI membership vector returned a Brier score of 0.0474, log loss 0.0805 and expected calibration error 0.0300, against 0.0479, 0.2771 and 0.0304 for gradient boosting on the richer seven-frequency input. The memberships were as well calibrated as gradient boosting and substantially better on log loss from less input, and their arg-max recovered the reference grade at kappa 0.9564, exceeding the 0.946 from the separately calibrated thresholds.

## Validation Under the WHO 2021 Schema

Under the 2021 schema the framework performed better on every metric except raw overall agreement (Table 4): kappa 0.959 against 0.946, mean absolute error 3.74 dB against 4.35, and rho 0.844 against 0.812. Borderline agreement was 88.0%, measured over the harder population, since the 2021 boundaries place 29.5% of ears within ±5 dB of one against 18.7%. Scoring the six-category system against the 2021 reference returned kappa 0.875.

## Decision-Curve Analysis

FAI-based referral maintained net benefit comparable to PTA-4-based referral across the threshold-probability range for both outcomes, and both exceeded treat-all at every threshold (Figure 3); for any hearing loss at a 10% threshold, net benefit was 0.126 against 0.131 and 0.034 for treating all. The small differences favour the crisp markers, which are defined on the outcome itself, so the substantive finding is that the graded index does not sacrifice decision utility.

## Transition-Width Ablation

Flooring the core gaps at 10 dB against the raw percentile gaps, which ranged from 5.7 to 13.6 dB, raised weighted kappa from 0.9266 to 0.9456 (+0.0190, 95% CI +0.0108 to +0.0272) and borderline agreement from 79.5% to 85.1% (+5.6 pp, 95% CI +2.8 to +8.5), both intervals excluding zero. Of the 152 ears (3.9%) the two widths labelled differently, the wider construction was correct 72.4% of the time against 24.3%.

Sweeping the floor from 4 to 16 dB in 2 dB steps showed the deployed setting sits on a plateau rather than a peak (Table 3): every floor from 6 to 12 dB was statistically indistinguishable from 10 dB, whereas 4 dB and 14 to 16 dB were significantly worse. Absolute error nevertheless fell monotonically with width, from 4.38 dB to 4.20 dB, so categorical and continuous agreement diverge at the wide end, wider shoulders smoothing the graded output while blurring the boundary. A 4 dB floor reproduces the raw-gap arm, so the percentile gaps were already about that wide.

## The Normal–Mild Transition

At the classic 25 dB cut-off the crisp rule flips the label between 26 and 27 dB with no graded information, whereas the system returns a smooth rise, so a 25 dB threshold is visibly closer to normal than a 27 dB one (Table S4).

## Clinical Case Studies

Four synthetic archetypes illustrate the framework (Figure 4). Case B is the most informative: a noise-induced notch with a normal PTA-4 of 22.5 dB returned FAI 21.2, while its configuration output identified a precipitous notched profile, flagging high-frequency pathology the severity grade alone misses.

# Discussion

## Principal Findings

A Mamdani fuzzy inference system was developed and validated that maps pure-tone thresholds onto a continuous index while preserving the information crisp classification discards. On held-out NHANES ears the FAI achieved weighted kappa 0.946 and matched the crisp grade in 99.1% of clear cases. Three findings stand out: the system remains compatible with standard practice; the graded representation is a better classifier than the calibrated label built on it, its arg-max reaching 0.9564; and the wider graded region improves rather than costs agreement, raising kappa by 0.019 and borderline agreement by 5.6 points with bootstrap intervals excluding zero.

## Agreement Cannot Evidence the Graded Representation

The probabilistic benchmark produced the study's most consequential result. A proportional-odds ordinal logistic regression recovered the reference grade exactly in all 3,912 test ears with a Brier score of zero, which is not a strong model but a proof that the label is a deterministic monotone function of the pure-tone average. Because the label is a thresholding, any model able to represent monotone thresholds recovers it exactly and agreement metrics saturate, so a graded representation cannot be shown to be better by kappa.

What survives is discrimination among approximations. Gradient boosting, on seven-frequency input with more capacity, scored kappa 0.9177 against 0.9564. A label defined by thresholds on one continuous quantity is what trapezoidal membership functions express natively, since the breakpoints are thresholds in decibels, whereas a tree ensemble must approximate the same step function through axis-aligned splits on noisy inputs. It is the probabilistic properties that discriminate, and there the memberships matched gradient boosting on Brier score and calibration error and halved its log loss, from the primary threshold alone.

## The Classification Schema Is a Parameter

The construction is not tied to the 25/40/55/70/90 boundaries, which trace to Clark rather than to WHO. The same cores, partition and calibration applied to the 2021 boundaries produced a better-calibrated system with lower absolute error, so the framework is schema-agnostic and agreement figures are interpretable only alongside the schema they were computed against. A change to WHO's grade table would require recalibration, not redesign.

## Clinical Implications

In audiologic triage the FAI could refine referral pathways by flagging patients who straddle severity boundaries, so a borderline case is monitored rather than forced into a category that misstates the loss. Prescriptive methods such as NAL-NL2 and DSL change compression ratios discretely at severity boundaries, whereas a configuration vector could guide frequency-specific amplification for notched or sloping patterns in which the PTA is a poor summary. For ototoxicity monitoring, the temporal tracking module flags sub-threshold FAI changes without a PTA boundary crossing, an early warning that conventional staging misses and that requires prospective validation.

## Comparison with Prior Work

The results are consistent with the computational audiology literature and qualify it. Machine-learning classifiers [@achakulvisut2025; @ceriani2025] achieve strong accuracy but are not inspectable, and clustering-based profiling [@saak2022; @saak2025] recovers phenotypes without offering an explicit decision a clinician can interrogate. This study adds that such comparisons are confounded when the target is a deterministic function of its inputs, and that graded outputs require proper scoring rules. No previously published fuzzy system integrates severity classification, configuration typing, asymmetry and temporal tracking in one inspectable framework validated with a participant-level split.

## Limitations

Only air-conduction thresholds were used, so the framework grades combined air-conduction loss and cannot separate sensorineural from conductive or mixed components; the complex-interaction rules therefore capture air-conduction contour rather than pathophysiological mixed loss. The rule base, though derived from audiology expertise, has not undergone formal Delphi consensus. The three cycles covered adults aged 20 to 69 years, so children and older adults are not represented, some configurations remain underrepresented, and extended high-frequency audiometry was not covered.

Inter-aural asymmetry was decoupled from severity during this work and now drives a referral recommendation instead. The rule base previously allowed asymmetry to upgrade severity, so an ear with a pure-tone average of 55 dB could be reported as moderately severe because the contralateral ear differed; asymmetry is a referral indicator rather than an amplifier of peripheral loss. The change is neutral for the figures reported here, since the single-ear protocol pins the asymmetry input to zero, but it aligns the validated rule base with the deployed one.

The World Report on Hearing [@who2021] lowered the normal boundary to 20 dB HL and added a complete-loss category. The reference standard used here, and the frequency band the severity rules share with it, mean agreement is partly by construction. The benchmark quantifies that dependence rather than removing it, since the exact reconstruction shows the ceiling is definitional. This limits what any agreement figure can mean, and is why the graded outputs and probabilistic metrics carry the argument. The case studies are synthetic archetypes rather than patient records. Whether the FAI predicts hearing-aid outcomes, patient-reported benefit or surgical candidacy has not been assessed.

## Generalizability and Future Directions

The framework is portable by design. Additional inputs can be accommodated by adding membership functions and rules, and a web-based calculator with a REST API for EHR integration has been deployed for clinical evaluation. Future work will validate the system prospectively, explore neuro-fuzzy approaches (ANFIS) that learn rule parameters while remaining interpretable, and test whether the graded index improves on the crisp grade in predicting speech-in-noise performance or hearing-aid outcomes.

## Conclusions

The Fuzzy Audiometric Index provides a continuous, frequency-resolved, interpretable classification of hearing loss that preserves the gradation lost to crisp thresholds. Validated on held-out NHANES ears, it shows substantial agreement with the reference classification while preserving information on borderline cases, configuration and graded severity. The probabilistic benchmark shows that the reference label is a deterministic thresholding of its input, so agreement cannot evidence the value of a graded representation; the membership vectors matched a gradient-boosted model on Brier score and calibration error and improved on log loss from less input.

# Figure Captions {.unnumbered}

**Figure 1.** Trapezoidal membership functions for the six hearing loss severity categories, arranged as a formal Ruspini partition. Successive functions share their feet with their neighbours' cores, so adjacent shoulders are complementary linear ramps that cross at 0.5 and memberships sum to 1 at every threshold across the 0 to 120 dB universe. Transition bands measure 13.6, 10.0, 10.0, 10.0 and 11.2 dB from normal to profound.
**Figure 2.** (a) Bland-Altman plot of the difference between FAI and PTA-4 against their mean on the held-out test set (bias +0.25 dB after mapping the index onto the decibel scale, 95% limits of agreement −11.2 to +11.7 dB). (b) Classification agreement as a function of distance from the nearest WHO severity boundary. The FAI matches the crisp grade on 99.1% of clear cases (≥6 dB from a boundary) and returns graded membership on 85.1% of borderline cases (±5 dB).
**Figure 3.** Decision-curve analysis on the held-out test set: net benefit of FAI-based referral versus PTA-4-based referral, the crisp reference grade rule, and treat-all/treat-none strategies, for (a) any hearing loss (≥ mild) and (b) moderate-or-worse loss. Risk models were fitted on the training partition.
**Figure 4.** Clinical case panels: four synthetic archetypes (A borderline mild, B noise notch, C presbycusis, D asymmetric) showing PTA versus FAI labels, membership bar plots and configuration vectors. Coloured background bands indicate WHO severity categories. Threshold arrays are given in Table S5.
